articles.title: Edinburgh launches new media event after final TV Festival ends
articles.text:
Plans for a new Scottish event to replace the Edinburgh TV Festival have been launched.

The industry festival – which ends on Friday – will move to Manchester next year after 50 years in the capital.

But Screen Scotland, the Scottish government and the other Edinburgh Festivals say it is too important to lose.

Speaking at a launch event in Edinburgh, Culture Secretary Màiri McAllan, revealed details of a new initiative which would build on the city's unique position as a global shop window for talent, content and creative ideas.

"We are so proud of Scotland's screen sector," she said. "And this exciting addition to the August festivals line-up will provide a new way to embrace the creativity and cultural innovation which makes our capital unique."

Initial research has already been undertaken with further consultation continuing under former TV festival creative director Rowan Woods.

It is hoped that a pilot version of the new festival will run in August 2027, and that it will be expanded to include those who consume content as well as those who make it.

McAllan said when she was first appointed culture secretary after the election in May, one of the first meetings she had was about the Edinburgh TV Festival.

"There was a collective disappointment about its departure but almost as soon as I was briefed on its departure, I was told 'don't worry minister, we're already on it. We will work together and move on'."

She said she was delighted to announce details of a new TV and screen festival for Edinburgh to sit alongside all the other festivals in August.

Richard Gadd, whose hit Netflix show Baby Reindeer was first discovered at the Edinburgh Festival Fringe told the event his first experience of the Fringe was with his school when they saw a production of Black Watch which was first staged there in 2006.

Four years later, he made his own debut with his solo show 6 And Half A 7 which was staged in a bar. Sometimes the audience was just one person, and he would just buy them a drink.

Later shows were more successful, including Monkey See, Monkey Do in 2016 which won him the Edinburgh Comedy award, and Baby Reindeer in 2019 which led to interest from TV executives from Netflix, BBC, C4 and HBO.

"Everything I have in my life, I owe to this festival, not just the chance to meet agents and producer writers but going full time as a writer," he said.

"A chance to experiment and take risks - to fail spectacularly and come back the next night to start again.

"If the fringe becomes too expensive, too commercial, we could lose the very thing which makes it extraordinary. We could lose the place where someone can arrive with an idea and leave with a career. "

Gadd pointed out that Fleabag, Taskmaster, Six the Musical, Rosencrantz and Guildenstern are Dead, Stomp, Flight of the Conchords, Garth Merengue, Alan Partridge, Mr Bean, The League of Gentlemen, Jerry Springer the Opera, Operation Mincemeat, The Mighty Boosh and Black Watch all began there.

"This is so much more than a festival," he said. "It's the cultural backbone of the whole country, the world even, and we must protect it at all costs so everyone who dares to step out their front door and call themselves an artist can be given the same opportunity that I was."

The TV festival began as the Edinburgh Television Drama festival in 1976 – a spin-off from the city's international film festival – founded by its director Linda Myles and Gus MacDonald, a former Granada TV executive.

Myles, the first woman to direct a major film festival was keen to spark ideas and debate about a rapidly changing industry.

Key to its success was its timing in the final week of the world's largest arts festival which allowed delegates to network, while also "shopping" the city for fresh ideas, talent and shows.

As well as Baby Reindeer, Fleabag was first performed as a theatre show before being developed by the BBC, as was Hannah Gadsby's show Nanette in 2017 before being developed by Netflix.

The various comedy awards handed out in the final week, also offer a shortlist for those attending the TV festival.

Since 2001, the TV festival has been run by an independent foundation based in London.

It attracts more than 2,000 delegates and retains some of the original features such as the MacTaggart lecture – named after the ground-breaking drama producer James MacTaggart who had died two years before.

Over the years, it has been delivered by Rupert Murdoch, Ted Turner, Vince Gallagher and David Attenborough.

TV dramatist and writer Dennis Potter used his moment in 1993 to lash out at the BBC's director general John Birt and chairman Marmaduke Hussey, calling them "croak-voiced Daleks" who had a cold and impersonal approach to TV writing.

Presenter Amol Rajan used his Alternative Mactaggart to urge the UK government to "stop dithering" about the BBC's funding structure.

The main lecture was delivered by Pedro Pina, Vice President of YouTube, who gave a reminder about the vast changes in the TV landscape since the festival first began.

But the wider festival ecosystem has also changed.

Concerns over affordability, accessibility and sustainability led to an offer to other UK cities to bid for the chance to host.

Edinburgh repeated its offer but was beaten by Manchester which will host the TV festival from 2027. Details of timings (since it no longer has to coincide with the last weeks of the festivals) and programme have yet to be announced.

There are few details about the Scottish replacement either, except that the consultation will be led by Rowan Woods and will be funded by Screen Scotland and delivered through the Fringe Society.

It is thought the ambition is to create an event which is not industry only, but opens out guest speakers who have included Shonda Rimes, Tina Fey and Gary Oldman, to audiences.

It will also expand its vision beyond traditional film and television output towards global content industries. Scotland has seen expanded interest in recent years with productions such as Outlander (Sony/Starz) and Dept Q (Netflix).

Separately, Screen Scotland plans to establish a new debate in honour of Linda Myles, who co-created that first TV festival.

The Linda Myles Debate will recognise her long-standing belief that Edinburgh is the place for rigorous debate around the screen industries.

"I'm deeply touched and honoured to have the debate named after me," she said.

"It's exciting to see the importance of ideas and discussion being recognised in the plans for the new event, especially as this was the initial intention of the creation of the Edinburgh Television Festival in 1976."

articles.title: ‘The whistling on the theme tune? That’s Dickie Attenborough!’ Hayley Mills on Whistle Down the Wind
articles.text:
Hayley Mills, played Kathy Bostock

Whistle Down the Wind was originally a novel written by my mother, Mary Hayley Bell, about three children living on a farm in Sussex. The children – loosely based on my sister Juliet, my brother Jonathan and myself – discover a man in their barn. Thinking he’s Jesus, they decide to hide him and protect him from the adults because they don’t want the same thing to happen to him as before.

Dickie Attenborough thought it was a wonderful story, and convinced my parents it should be made into a film by the production company he’d set up with the actor and writer Bryan Forbes. After the original director, Guy Green, pulled out, Bryan took over at the 11th hour. He’d never directed before. When Dickie asked if he could do it, he apparently said: “I’ve no idea. We’ll soon find out!”

Keith Waterhouse and Willis Hall were engaged as writers and made the brilliant decision to move the story to a remote part of Lancashire. The perfect location was found in the village of Downham, at the foot of Pendle Hill, famous for the witch hunts. Nearly all of the children in the film were local: the only experienced child actors were Roy Holder, who played Jackie, and me. I was 14 and a head and shoulders taller than most of the other kids. The sleeves on my coat were too short and my arms stuck out like a scarecrow’s.

I’d just made two films in America for Disney. Shooting on a Lancashire farm in winter was very different: there was mud everywhere, and we often had to walk very carefully on duckboards. But I always loved filming in England. We’d be eating dripping, jam butties and fried eggs in a bun. Bryan was great at communicating what he wanted from the children without just getting them to parrot him. In the scene where the boy slaps me in the playground, the hand in the closeup was actually Bryan’s. He really whacked me! Kathy isn’t supposed to show that she’s been affected, so it wasn’t until cameras stopped rolling that I cried.

Arthur Ibbetson’s black and white cinematography wonderfully captured the stark, leafless trees and the mist blowing across the hills. It had a sort of film noir quality, and as a child I loved the night shoots. This was all beautifully complemented by Malcolm Arnold’s poignant, nostalgic music. His arrangement of We Three Kings was a perfect fit for the kids’ tiny figures leaping like hares on the brow of the hill – and that’s Dickie himself whistling on the main theme.

I’ve always said Alan Barnes stole the show as my little brother, Charles. He was only seven. The first morning on location, there was a row of director’s chairs with the names of adult cast and crew members on them. He pointed at Alan Bates’s chair and said, “Ey up, they’ve spelled me name wrong.” By the next day, the props department had made a tiny chair just for him. One of his lines became the most quoted one from the film: “It isn’t Jesus. It’s just a fella.” He delivered it perfectly.

Diane Poole (nee Holgate), played Nan Bostock

I was 10 when Bryan and Richard visited my school. I didn’t know who they were. The head teacher just said two men would be coming to the playground to watch us play, but not to bother about it. Afterwards, a few of us were grouped together and told the men were looking for children to be in a film. When I told my mum, she said: “Don’t be so ridiculous and get your dinner eaten.” But the next day Richard Attenborough turned up at the front door. She was horrified as it was a Wednesday – and she wasn’t due to scrub the front step until Friday.

I remember doing a screen test up at the farm where a lot of the film was made. We just had to look round the end of a stone wall and say, “Is he coming?” without looking at the camera. I’d done school plays before and played Snow White, which involved learning quite a lot of dialogue, so this seemed easy.

Nan wasn’t the child who didn’t believe, and she wasn’t the one who was totally besotted. She kept the peace between the other two. I was probably a quiet child at home: I guess they saw that in my personality. Bryan kept some of our mistakes in the film, which helps make it feel more real. In one scene, I spell “Bible” wrong and in another I mispronounce “Christmas”.

In those days, us kids didn’t go to the cinema so I didn’t know who Hayley Mills was. She was like a real big sister, though, and we would act the goat together. It was only when we went to Pinewood to film scenes set inside the farmhouse that we started seeing what footage had been shot. It was a revelation. We thought: “Oh, this is what it’s all about.” They borrowed the actual back door from the real farmhouse to use on the set. My dad had a haulage firm and got one of his drivers to deliver it.

Alan Bates was very pleasant and softly spoken, so in the scene where he suddenly shouts at the “disciples”, we thought: “Oh crikey, what have we done?” At the London premiere, he came up and swung me around and I didn’t recognise him until he spoke, because he’d shaved his beard off. I got sent to Harrods to choose a dress for the London premiere, but I insisted on wearing the one my granny had bought me.

The scene I’m most proud of is when Kathy first tells Nan about Jesus being in the barn, while they’re in bed together. That was the last thing I did at Pinewood and by then I’d got used to it all. It was a long scene, but looking at it now I think: “Yeah, you did all right there, kid.”

A new 35mm print of Whistle Down the Wind screens at the BFI Southbank, London, on 4 September, with a Q&A with Hayley Mills, Diane Poole and Alan Barnes. A BFI Film Classic book, Whistle Down the Wind, is published on 3 September

articles.title: Reading and Leeds festival review – post-GCSE blowout shows how dominant dance music now is
articles.text:
Reading and Leeds festival will probably always be a post-GCSE rite of passage: a gleefully riotous taste of freedom before having to make actual life decisions. But the sibling events have been struggling for a sense of identity beyond this, particularly post-Covid. In 2025, the festival decided to theme days based on genre, which felt out of touch – but, this year, organisers have decided to tackle gen Z’s borderless approach head on. There are new stages, such as the chandelier-adorned Ballroom, and overall the lineup is wonderfully mazy.

On the festival’s second stage, you can catch everything from UK rap and garage selector DJ EJ, warbly US rockers Geese, and raw, live-drummed jungle from 4am Kru. “I dedicate this one to all the bad bitches from small places. Let’s make a song about the bad bitches from Leeds,” Slovakian pop star Adéla gleefully giggles during her own set here, before launching into neon-streaked megahit Ain’t in LA. In a ping-ponging journey across styles, other highlights include London singer Dexter in the Newsagent’s blue-skied bedroom pop, Australian artist Mall Grab’s Game Boy grime beats and Bar Italia’s insouciant rock, which is significantly more fun and dance-y than their recent lukewarm album reviews might suggest.

Thursday is headlined by a tired-sounding Kasabian, who don’t move a crowd of kids that, for good reason, would much rather be at LS23, the trippy dance stage in the woods. Chase and Status’ festival-sized drum’n’bass scratches that dance itch as Friday’s main stage headliner, while Charli xcx (reviewed in full here) and Fontaines DC are a spellbinding double bill on Saturday. The latter play new material from their forthcoming album Dopamine Chamber, including beguiling single Marianne, and an unreleased new track called Happy for You – it’s driven by a Sundays-sounding guitar line and a peppy rimshot, but moves with melancholy, the band members’ features obscured against a humming green light onstage. Their set is the best from a guitar band all weekend.

Another new stage, the Canopy, replaces the BBC Introducing stage at both festivals and is a showcase of new artists curated by Festival Republic, who are majority owned by Live Nation – it has been dubbed the “nepo baby” stage for platforming the offspring of Dave Grohl, Liam Gallagher and the Beckhams. For the most part, the programming is disastrously bad, and the stage is underattended until festivalgoers can catch a perfunctory glimpse of someone semi-famous. Then it swarms, making sets look like a moment that doesn’t actually exist from the outside, and to the detriment of other artists who would benefit from not being juxtaposed with celebrities’ kids. The two best acts are young alt-rock four-piece Tooth and brilliantly talented singer Sade Olutola, and yet they only get 20-minute opening slots on the Saturday and Sunday.

If Reading and Leeds can be defined by anything this past year, it is young people’s ongoing affinity for tech house DJs like Josh Baker, Omar+, Max Dean and Luke Dean; Irish producer Kettama’s set is one of the most packed-out of the weekend. These artists play perfectly engineered going-out music, with chantable vocal samples and mixes that build and change a little too fast, like doomscrolling in audio form.

The dance music is mainly on the Warehouse stage, which is not unlike a mockup of Manchester’s Warehouse Project, and is where the most crowd energy is directed across the weekend. Issues with overcrowding mean that Silva Bumpa and a Skepta b2b with Prospa are cancelled, with calls online for Reading and Leeds to recognise the popularity of dance and move it to bigger stages. Baker clashes with Dave on Sunday, and despite cameos from Kano and Central Cee, the Dave crowd is by far the most sparse out of all the headliners.

You can really see Reading and Leeds’ transformation at Hedex’s set, when the drum’n’bass DJ drops a mix that begins with a sped-up version of Nirvana’s Smells Like Teen Spirit. There’s a slight bit of confusion at a tune that once embodied this festival. Still, the crowd join in singing the verse, before Hedex pulverises the track to the same effect as the distorted drop in the original and everyone’s back to dancing with that same immediacy, that same teenage freedom.

articles.title: Gen Z ‘Chinamaxxers’ fantasise about life in China. This journalist and this artist can never go back there
articles.text:
Drinking Tsingtao beers, eating congee, walking with hands behind their backs: for many young people in western countries, “Chinamaxxing” has become all the rage. Some content creators have even gone beyond the jokes about being in “a very Chinese time in my life” and have followed this passion to the Middle Kingdom: making TikToks in Chongqing’s multi-layered metropolis, bathing in Chengdu’s 24-hour spas, or backflipping on the Great Wall of China.

This irreverent, mostly ironic trend is jarring for some, but Chinese-Australian artist Badiucao and Chinese-American journalist Melissa Chan don’t want to lecture the so-called Chinamaxxers.

“The younger generation feel like there is no meaningful method to change society. They feel defeated when they see what’s happening in Gaza – there’s been protests but the government doesn’t care and is collaborating with atrocities in wars. There’s also the Epstein files in America, which show how the elite is corrupt,” says Badiucao, who, along with Chan, is in Sydney to promote their new book, You Must Take Part in Revolution.

“When you want to see change, there is the hard way, which is being innovative and finding a solution. And there is the lazy way, which is finding a cheap alternative and fantasising about a faraway, oriental, communist country that might be your future,” he says.

Chan and Badiucao have both paid the price for criticising China’s one-party system. Chinese officials refused to renew Chan’s press credentials before expelling the former Al Jazeera journalist from China in 2012; and the previously anonymous political cartoonist Badiucao was forced to reveal his identity in 2019 after it was compromised and authorities threatened his family in China.

You Must Take Part in Revolution, the pair’s debut graphic novel, portrays a dystopian future where China is at war with the United States in 2035.

The graphic novel features a variety of characters from the Chinese-speaking diaspora, including from Hong Kong, Taiwan, the US and Tibet, as they decide what choices they are willing to make under authoritarian oppression.

“It was intentional to show the panoply of Asian identities that have been impacted by a great power,” Chan says. “It opens up the possibility to get young people to better understand it’s not just a ‘Chinese time in my life’, that there’s a lot going on here … hopefully it can get a few people thinking about resistance movements both present and in the past.”

“We don’t want to just lecture,” Badiucao adds. “We really want readers to put themselves in the eyes of those characters as if they were a real human being with a real life.”

Chan now lives in Berlin and has written for the Atlantic, the Washington Post, Time, and others, while Badiucao, who lives in Melbourne, has exhibited works across the world. They started working on the graphic novel five years ago after first meeting in Germany during the late 2010s.

You Must Take Part in Revolution starts off in the real-life Hong Kong protests of 2019, when almost two million people took to the streets to denounce a controversial law that would allow the extradition of suspects to mainland China. The law was viewed as a sign of growing mainland influence in Hong Kong.

While the graphic novel is geographically grounded in an Asia governed by authoritarian China, it also portrays the US as a proto-fascist state, resisting the idea that criticising one necessarily means painting the other in a positive light.

“This book happens to focus on China, but authoritarianism everywhere is bad,” Chan says. “We don’t want anyone to engage in whataboutism and I don’t think there needs to be a balance – if things are shit, they’re shit in any country.”

Unlike other graphic novels such as Art Spiegelman’s Maus, Badiucao and Chan’s book takes its influence from Japanese manga. “There are great works like Attack on Titan which are not necessarily about specific history or political content that have so many metaphors reflecting important things like racism, war and equity,” Badiucao says.

“It’s part of the reason this form is potentially more than just entertainment or some kid stuff, it really influences an entire generation.”

You Must Take Part in Revolution was released in the US and UK in 2025, but it is only just getting its Australian release this week.

Badiucao says readers across the world have contacted them about their own histories after reading it, including Ukrainian refugees who have escaped Russia’s invasion, and Czech communities who lived through the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic.

The artist recalls one interaction at a comic festival in New York, where a second-generation Chinese Canadian girl told him that she had hesitations about taking the book home. “I don’t think my mum would love it,” she said.

A few minutes later, an older woman came up to Badiucao and explained she was an immigrant whose family had been through hardship during the Cultural Revolution. Flipping through the book, she said her daughter might like it, but she didn’t know if she would be open to learning about Chinese politics.

Badiucao later discovered the two were mother and daughter.

“I told the daughter her mum might be more open about political stuff, and I told the mum that your daughter might be interested too,” he says. “They ended up having an honest conversation, and they got a copy of the book … among all the interactions with readers, that was pretty special to me.”
